John Stuart Mill. A nineteenth century British philosopher and economist who synthesized David Ricardo's political economy with utilitarian ethics, arguing that the purpose of economics is to maximize human happiness.

Mill wrote Principles of Political Economy in 1848, which became the standard textbook of its era. He refined Ricardian economics but added a crucial humane dimension. Yes, he said, there are laws of production that work like laws of nature. You cannot repeal the law of gravity or the arithmetic of economics. But the laws of distribution are different. Distribution depends on social institutions and customs and arrangements that humans have created, and therefore can change.

He grounded economics in utilitarianism, the principle that the aim of all policy is the greatest happiness for the greatest number. This ethical foundation gave economics a moral purpose beyond merely describing how markets work. He championed progressive taxation, public education, and limits on property rights to reduce inequality. These were radical ideas for their time, proposing to use government power to reshape economic distribution toward greater fairness.

Mill was equally passionate about women's rights. He wrote The Subjection of Women in 1869, arguing for women's legal equality and voting rights. He believed women should have the same educational and economic opportunities as men. This was far ahead of its time.

He served in Parliament and was a major public intellectual across politics, philosophy, and economics. He extended Adam Smith's moral philosophy and free-trade vision with a utilitarian framework that asked not just whether markets clear, but whether they serve human flourishing. Later, John Maynard Keynes admired Mill's ethical approach to economics and his skepticism of laissez-faire absolutes. Karl Marx, his contemporary, also critiqued capitalism, but from the opposite direction. Where Mill sought to reform capitalism through greater fairness and education, Marx believed revolution was necessary to overthrow it entirely.
